title: In one MICrONS mouse, higher visual areas had steeper movie response spectra inside 13 scans but not clearly in pooled scans; simple stimulus features and behavior did not explain it
abstract: We tested in an independent data set whether response spectra decay faster in higher mouse visual areas, as found in Allen data. We used MICrONS mouse 17797: 13 two-photon scans, 104,171 units in V1, LM, RL and AL, and six identical 10-s natural movie clips with 5 to 10 repeats. The cvPCA estimator and decision rule were fixed before area spectra were calculated. Inside scans (200 units per area), alpha rose along the anatomical hierarchy: V1 0.906, LM 0.950, RL 0.945, AL 1.021; mean slope 0.226 (0.129 to 0.323), positive in 11 of 13 scans. This is similar to Allen values for the same areas. The slope stayed after reliability and depth matching and with other bin sizes, and decreased to 0.132 after receptive-field position matching. In 300-unit populations pooled across scans the slope was only 0.052 (scan bootstrap -0.021 to 0.263), so the pre-registered pooled criterion failed. Exploratory tests showed why: V1 alpha did not change when units came from more scans, but higher-area alpha fell. The dominant stimulus directions of higher areas were specific to the scan. This was not explained by recording day, behavior, depth, receptive-field position or local plane signals, and it also occurred in the MICrONS digital twin on 4,999 new frames, where the area order held (alpha 0.77, 0.83, 0.84). Higher areas held more variance in global luminance, contrast and motion-energy subspaces, but removal of these subspaces or of shared higher-area directions did not decrease the slope. Removal of dominant V1 directions increased it. Slower temporal integration explained about 40% of the higher-area excess. Limits: one mouse, four areas, 216 stimulus points, exploratory post-hoc diagnostics. Code, aggregate results, figures and exact provenance are included; MICrONS data stay external.
